# Projective Texture Mapping
## Overview
Projective texture mapping assigns solid textures to volume objects by connecting 3D positions to 2D projective positions on a plenoptic surface, and then to integral coordinates in a morphed texture image [S1, unofficial]. It solves the problem of intermixing volumetric rendering with solid texturing without requiring explicit geometric parameterization of the volume [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
The method operates on a plenoptic surface parameterized by continuous variables $u \in [0, 1]$ and $v \in [0, 1]$ [S1, unofficial]. It uses a regular bounding shape (sphere, cylinder, or box) enclosing the volume as the projection target [S1, unofficial]. The core mechanism involves two phases: forward projection to generate multi-resolution intermediate templates, and inverse projection to map textures from a morphed image onto the volume [S1, unofficial].

For an intermediate template with dimensions $x_d \times y_d$, resolution intervals are $\Delta u = 1/(x_d - 1)$ and $\Delta v = 1/(y_d - 1)$ [S1, unofficial]. A pixel at continuous position $(u, v)$ is indexed by integral pair $(x, y)$ where $u = x \cdot \Delta u$ and $v = y \cdot \Delta v$ [S1, unofficial].

For a voxel $p(X, Y, Z)$, a ray is cast through the point and the plenoptic primitive centroid $(O_x, O_y, O_z)$ [S1, unofficial]. The ray determines the 2D projective position $(u, v)$ on the plenoptic surface, which maps to integral coordinates in a high-resolution patch of the morphed texture image [S1, unofficial].

The resolution of the morphed texture image directly impacts accuracy; higher resolutions reduce aliasing artifacts known as the "cliff effect" [S1, unofficial]. The cliff effect occurs when a single pixel projected onto a surface almost parallel to the direction of projection is smeared over a relatively large area [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Multi-constraints-based projective texture mapping](12075-multi-constraints-based-projective-texture-mapping.md)
This method places textures on iso-surfaces by warping a source texture to align with user-defined key points on an intermediate template, then rendering via ray-casting. It solves the problem of ill-conditioned direct projection by using spatial and semantic constraints (transfer functions) to control texture position. Unlike traditional mesh-based mapping, it does not require filling topological holes; regions with artefacts receive the same texture as their radial neighborhood. It uses data-dependent triangulation for interpolation to retain edge quality, superior to standard bilinear interpolation.

### [Projective Space Texture Mapping with Multi-Resolution Templates](13236-projective-space-texture-mapping-with-multi-resolution-templ.md)
This technique assigns solid textures to any position within a volume using plenoptic projection functions as pseudo-procedure functional models. It connects 3D positions to 2D projective positions on a plenoptic surface, and then to integral coordinates in a morphed texture image. It is distinguished by its use of multi-resolution intermediate templates generated via forward projection (DVR/DSR) and inverse projection to mitigate aliasing artifacts.

### High-Resolution Patching
**Definition:** A technique to overcome resolution limitations by directly importing a high-resolution image (patch) for a specific portion of the morphed texture image during texture mapping [S1, unofficial].
**Steps:** Import a high-resolution texture image (patch) during texture mapping, with or without morphing, to replace or composite with the low-resolution area [S1, unofficial]. Fine-tune the inverse projection to an extremely small area to digitally composite textures using different texture images (e.g., cliff texture and horse leg texture) [S1, unofficial].
**Details:** In a horse-on-cliff experiment, the paint area in the low-resolution texture was $66 \times 20$ pixels, while the high-resolution horse image was $256 \times 166$ pixels [S1, unofficial]. Using the high-res patch preserved details, whereas the low-res patch suffered from alias artifacts and detail loss [S1, unofficial]. The projective space texture is defined in continuous 3D space, allowing the inverse projection to be fine-tuned to an extremely small area to composite textures [S1, unofficial].

### MVS-Texturing
**Definition:** Classical texturing baseline that projects training images as textures onto a CAD mesh [S2, unofficial].
**Pitfalls:** Produces patchwork textures with visible seams [S2, unofficial]. Fails on wide-baseline views, causing abrupt transitions, misalignment artifacts, holes, and missing parts [S2, unofficial]. Test-time refinement causes divergence [S2, unofficial].
**Metrics:** Six-scene average PSNR: 11.77, mPSNR: 14.64, fgPSNR: 6.83 [S2, unofficial].

## Background
The method originates from the work of P. Shen and P. Willis, published in "Texture Mapping Volume Objects" [S1, unofficial].

## Sources
[S1] Texture Mapping Volume Objects, https://doi.org/10.2312/vvg.20051006, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)
